planting.note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type carrot bred to hold good sweetness even when sown or harvested in warm weather, a real advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat usually turns carrots bitter and woody.

directions: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2-4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2-3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall. Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type hybrid carrot specifically noted for retaining good, consistent sweetness even when grown through warmer weather than most carrots tolerate well, since heat typically pushes carrots toward a stronger, more bitter flavor and woody texture. The smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange with a small core and crisp, juicy texture. In zone 8-9, sow in late winter for an early spring harvest and again in late summer for a fall crop, and expect Nelson to hold its sweet flavor through a wider harvest window than standard carrot varieties.

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Valley Girl carries resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt, and is especially noted for continuing to set fruit under heat stress that causes many other tomatoes to drop blossoms — a strong match for Gulf South summers.

directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous semi-determinate vines; Valley Girl combines resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt with an unusually reliable ability to set fruit under heat stress, when high nighttime temperatures cause many tomato varieties to drop their blossoms without setting fruit. It produces medium-sized (6-8 oz), round, deep red fruit with well-balanced, classic tomato flavor over a long harvest season. Because it keeps fruiting through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer that stalls many other varieties, Valley Girl helps bridge the gap between the spring and fall tomato crops. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color and keep the vines picked regularly to encourage continued production.

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Jasper is a 2013 All-America Selections winner and one of the only cherry tomatoes resistant to both early and late blight along with Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, a rare disease package that suits the humid, blight-prone Gulf South growing season.

directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines; Jasper was named an All-America Selections winner for being one of the very few cherry tomatoes with resistance to both early and late blight, alongside resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, giving it an outstanding disease package for humid, disease-prone gardens. It produces heavy, extended clusters of small, deep red, exceptionally sweet cherry fruit with a crack-resistant skin that holds up on the vine. Because it keeps healthy foliage even under the fungal disease pressure that builds in a wet Gulf Coast summer, Jasper tends to remain productive well after less resistant cherry tomatoes have declined. Pick fruit as clusters ripen to full red color and harvest regularly to keep the vine setting new flowers.
sources: All-America Selections — Jasper tomato AAS winner 2013

common_name: Red Racer Tomato (Nematode-Resistant AAS-Winning Cocktail Hybrid)

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Racer is a 2018 All-America Selections winner bred with high resistance to Fusarium wilt, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt — the nematode resistance is especially valuable in the sandy, nematode-prone soils common along the Gulf Coast.

directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F; Red Racer is a compact, determinate cocktail-sized tomato recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally early maturity and broad disease resistance, including root-knot nematodes, a soil pest that stunts and weakens tomato roots and is a persistent problem in the sandy soils common across the Gulf Coast. It produces an early, concentrated crop of round, deep red, 2-3 ounce fruit with good, well-balanced flavor on plants compact enough for containers or small raised beds. Because of its resistance to nematodes as well as Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt, Red Racer performs reliably even in garden soil where other tomatoes have struggled. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color for the best flavor.
sources: All-America Selections — Red Racer tomato AAS winner 2018

planting.note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Rebelski carries a comprehensive disease-resistance package — Fusarium crown and root rot, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, powdery mildew, several races of leaf mold, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt — originally bred for greenhouse and high-tunnel production but valuable for the heavy disease pressure of Gulf South gardens.

directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or trellis the tall, vigorous indeterminate vines; Rebelski was bred for greenhouse and high-tunnel growers and carries one of the broadest disease-resistance packages available in a beefsteak-type tomato, including Fusarium crown and root rot, Fusarium wilt, powdery mildew, multiple races of leaf mold, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt. It produces large, crack-resistant, deep red beefsteak fruit with excellent classic tomato flavor on a plant that continues setting fruit reliably even under heavy disease pressure. In an open Gulf South garden, this extensive resistance package helps the vines stay productive later into the humid summer than most beefsteak varieties. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color and keep vines pruned and tied to their support for the best air circulation and fruit quality.
